title: Learning from rejection
content:
If you’re doing something creative, something important or something new, you’re certain to be rejected along the way.

It’s a signal. It might be proof that you offered it to the wrong person, or that the right person saw something about your work that didn’t serve their needs. Without learning from this signal, we’re doomed to experience it again and again.

What do we know for sure?

_It was rejected._

What else?

Nothing. The reasons listed in the rejection letter are almost certainly made up. Perhaps they’re insulating themselves from being re-sold (“you said you didn’t like the color, but we have other colors!”) or perhaps they’re protecting your feelings. It could be that they aren’t telling themselves the truth, or don’t want to be hassled for telling you the truth.

Few people explain their rejection with, “I’m afraid,” or “I wanted to do it but my boss won’t let me,” or “you have bad breath and I don’t like you.”

Being rejected hurts, and we’re likely to marinate in the pain. We imagine that the person who rejected us understands everything about what we offered, is a rational actor and cares as much as we do. While we’re at it, we personalize, amplify and multiply the rejection.

But all we really know is that this person, on this day, in this situation, hearing the story the way we told it, said no.

Years ago, I self-published a booklet for political activists. My timing was good, and I had a chance to sell the books from an organizer’s booth at a march on the very topic my book was about. It was a beautiful April day, and I stood on the side of route as the march went by. More than 400,000 passed my table, and I sold four books.

That’s 399,996 rejections. Maybe more.

Was it the price? Halfway through the march, I lowered it from $10 to $1, just to have a good story to blog a few decades later.

Sales did not increase. Perhaps it was the color of the jacket, the page count or the typo on page 32? None of those things.

What did I learn? That people at a march are at the march to march, not to shop.

Watch what people do, not what they say. And if you really want to learn something, change the situation and see what happens the next time.

Learning from rejection begins with understanding the lesson that’s being offered.

title: Scientists Catch a Rare Glimpse of a Fish With a See-Through Head
content:
The barreleye fish—also known as the spookfish—is one of the strangest-looking critters in the ocean. The front of its head is semi-transparent, giving observers a clear look into its internal anatomy.

It's not a fish that gets observed very often, though, which is why scientists are so excited about newly captured footage from the depths of the Monterey Canyon in the Pacific Ocean. Around 20 minutes of 4K video was recorded by a remotely operated vehicle (ROV) nearly 2,000 feet below the surface off the coast of California.

[Video 7](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nyldZ7BB_cE)

The ROV was operated by a team from the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute (MBARI), and it was on its way back to the surface after a filming session when the barreleye was spotted in the murky waters.

It’s the first time the fish (_Macropinna microstoma_) has been spotted by MBARI researchers since 2021, and only the 11th occasion in approximately 7,000 dives by the ROV. The creature lives in what’s known as the twilight zone, which starts at 656 feet down. There’s not enough light for photosynthesis down there, so you won’t find plant life.

A view from inside the MBARI control room. _Credit: MBARI_

“Seeing a barreleye fish is a rare treat,” MBARI’s Steven Haddock said in a [statement](https://www.mbari.org/news/mbari-researchers-film-rarely-seen-deep-sea-barreleye-fish-in-4k/). “Crew from across the ship joined the science team in the control room, mesmerized by this remarkable animal. Deep-sea animals capture the imagination, creating wonder and awe that we hope will inspire stewardship of the largest living space on Earth.”

The transparent portion of the fish’s body means its eyes can be inside its head, looking around in all directions—but especially upward—for the silhouettes of prey to snack on. Another benefit of the see-through tissue around the eyes is the protection it provides the barreleye against the stinging tentacles of siphonophores, the spindly organisms from which the fish is known to steal food.

Getting such a close-up look at the barreleye will help researchers better understand how vision works at these depths and how the fish evolved to become so bizarre in terms of appearance.

“_Macropinna_ reminds us of the surprising ways that animals have adapted to thrive in the ocean’s midwater,” added Haddock. “So many of them survive by looking for subtle optical cues, like a shadow passing overhead, and this sets off evolutionary competition, pitting bioluminescent camouflage against increasingly sophisticated visual capabilities.”

Sometimes the survival of the fittest is also survival of the most anatomically creative. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: How the Brain’s Failing Trash Compactor Can Contribute to Alzheimer’s Disease
content:
It seems like every other day a new report comes out linking another gene variant to Alzheimer’s disease.

_CASS4_, a member of a family of scaffold genes, is one of these genes. As far as genes go, its function seems fairly mundane. It codes for a protein involved in intracellular infrastructure and adhesion. However, several studies have tied single nucleotide polymorphisms in _CASS4_ to an increased risk of developing Alzheimer’s. Now a new study [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.1084/jem.20260104) in the _Journal of Experimental Medicine_ is helping explain why.

“Despite _CASS4_ being an Alzheimer’s risk gene, really nothing is known about what this gene does or how it affects the brain during disease,” study author Addie Walsh of the University of Virginia explained in a [statement](https://www.uvahealth.com/news/alzheimer-s-discovery-reveals-brain-cleaning-gone-wrong). “Our lab sought to address this major knowledge gap with this paper.”

Walsh and a team of neuroscientists used mice as a model organism to study the gene. They crossed transgenic mice with no _CASS4_ gene with transgenic mice engineered to manifest amyloid plaques, clumps of sticky beta-amyloid protein that build up in the brains of those with Alzheimer’s. They then put their offspring through a battery of tests to investigate the activity of _CASS4_.

The mice had larger and more numerous amyloid plaques in their brains and more damaged neurons, and cognitive tests showed they struggled to form new memories. To zoom in at the cellular level, the team looked at how the loss of _CASS4_ affected the brain cells where they were expressed: microglia. These are the brain’s resident immune cells, responsible for clearing toxins, fighting pathogens, and clearing away dead cells. Essentially they’re the brain’s little trash collectors.

Curiously, the lack of _CASS4_ didn’t make the microglia any less numerous, active, or worse at collecting amyloid. When microglia are functioning normally, they surround the plaques, forming a protective barrier and compacting them. But without _CASS4_, they struggled to do this important job.

According to the team, these findings may allow doctors to detect Alzheimer’s sooner—an important development considering currently available pharmaceuticals only slow the disease down—and could lead to new treatments. “Our work further suggests that defective _CASS4_ activity may serve as an early-onset biomarker to detect Alzheimer’s and that therapeutic strategies which boost its function may offer a much-needed approach to treat this devastating brain disease,” study author John Lukens said.

It could also advance treatments for other diseases. _CASS4_ isn’t just linked to Alzheimer’s; it’s been implicated in lung cancer, cystic fibrosis, thrombosis, and more.

Genes with mundane jobs can cause a lot of damage when something goes wrong. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: What’s All That Coffee Doing to Your Gut?
content:
It’s a real blessing that coffee is mostly good for us. This unique cocktail of bioactive compounds is an extremely popular beverage, and its health benefits range from mood-boosting to reducing mortality. (Of course, even if it were bad for our health, we’d probably drink it daily anyway.) Still, we don’t know that much about what habitual coffee drinking actually does to the gut.

And so, to find out, a team of nutritional scientists from the University of Copenhagen sent an electronic pill on a fantastic voyage through the digestive system of both coffee lovers and infrequent coffee drinkers. On its journey, the SmartPill® was busy measuring the temperature, pH levels, and intestinal contractions. The researchers also analyzed urine and stool samples from the participants, both to get a better measure of their coffee intake and to analyze their gut flora.

**Read more: “**[**How Coffee Affects Your Sex Hormone Levels**](https://nautil.us/how-coffee-affects-your-sex-hormone-levels-1283854)**”**

They discovered that habitual coffee drinkers—that is, those who drank one to five cups on at least three days of the eight-day study period—had a greater diversity of microorganisms living in their guts compared to the infrequent coffee drinkers. Javaheads also had a markedly reduced pH level (or a more acidic environment) in their small intestines. “But perhaps more importantly, frequent coffee consumption appears to affect the physiology of the gut itself, in other words how the gut functions,” study author Francesca Bucci explained in a [statement](https://www.eurekalert.org/news-releases/1151101).

Specifically, they found that habitual coffee drinkers experienced more colon contractions. While this particular piece of data may seem like something you’ve uncovered independently through your daily morning experiments with the substance, it’s not so cut-and-dry. Transit time, or the time it took the SmartPill® to wind its way through the digestive tract, was similar for both groups. Basically, both trains ran on schedule, but the coffee track came with more jostling.

While the researchers say the pH findings are too preliminary to determine whether or not they’re good for us, the findings on gut contractions are more straightforward. “Contractions in the gut can support healthy digestion, help prevent constipation, and keep the intestinal muscles in good condition,” Bucci said.

The sample size for the study (especially the infrequent drinkers) was rather small, but the researchers stress it was more exploratory in nature. Additional research could open up new avenues of treatments for those who suffer from intestinal disorders. “If we can understand how coffee affects digestion and intestinal contractions, it may be possible to use that knowledge to stimulate gut motility in a natural way,” study author Henrik Munch Roager explained. “That would be extremely valuable.”

I’ll raise a mug to that. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Four Forces That Shape Collective Memory
content:
Physicist César Hidalgo has been studying who becomes famous and what shapes our collective memory of popular figures for over a decade. What makes someone like Napoleon a household name across the world, whereas Bernando O’Higgins, a Chilean military officer who helped to lead that nation’s successful battle for independence, is only recognized within a small corner of South America? How did the rise of printing, television and other technologies shape who we tell stories about and remember for decades to come?

A pioneer in the field of economic complexity, Hidalgo’s interest arose in part out of his work on a project called the Observatory of Economic Complexity, which uses trade data to map out the commercial goods different countries make and sell to one another. He wondered if there might also be a way to trace the cultural products that countries produce and spread around the globe—and the forces that drive these scientific, intellectual, and artistic currents. So in 2013, he created another online observatory called [pantheon.world](https://pantheon.world/), a repository of collective cultural memory.

**Read more:**[**“How We’ll Forget John Lennon”**](https://nautil.us/how-well-forget-john-lennon-237297)

In Pantheon, famous people are a proxy for cultural products because biographical data is easy to organize, he says. You can see, for example, that Brazil has produced globally recognized musicians, race car drivers, soccer players, and architects. And you can see exactly who they are: say, bossa nova great [Antônio Carlos Jobim](https://www.google.com/search?kgmid=%2Fm%2F01rf_w&q=Ant%C3%B4nio+Carlos+Jobim) or Ayrton Senna, considered one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history. “Since then, we have been exploring the forces that shape collective memory, that shape that shared information that we carry about the past,” says Hidalgo.

Recently, Hidalgo and colleagues from the United States and Europe published a new [study](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/10/pgag308/8825253?searchresult=1&login=true) that looks at how our place of residence and language shape who sticks in our collective memory—both locally around the globe. It is one of a series of studies he and colleagues have published over the years that aim to capture the dimensions of collective memory. I recently spoke with Hidalgo about collective amnesia, “sleeping beauties,” localism, and how large language models may influence what we remember and what we forget.

**You grew up in Chile, but later lived in the United States and now in France. I actually lived in Chile for five years in my 20s and missed out on certain aspects of U.S. culture during that time, something I still sometimes notice in certain conversations. How does leaving****one’s country of origin shape a person’s relationship to collective memory?**

Yes, I grew up in Chile, and I was a very curious young man who wanted to learn about the world, so I was a voracious reader. In the ’80s, we would get these local newspaper supplements about science and technology, where I would read about Michael Faraday and Charles Darwin and so forth.

One of the things that was very apparent to me when I was reading about all of these people who had contributed to knowledge in physics and knowledge in the arts is that none of them were Chilean. It became very obvious that if you wanted to contribute to that type of intellectual life, you had to join that club, that sort of international global milieu.

The only people in Chile who got close to that were people who left Chile at some point, like Pablo Neruda, who won a Nobel Prize, as a poet, but spent much of his life in France and other parts of the world. Musicians from Chile, like Los Jaivas, also spent a lot of time in France. Even the most famous actors from Chile, like Pedro Pascal, left Chile as an infant, and made it big in the United States.

There was this other part of the story, which is that in some way the ceiling of what you can achieve culturally depends on where you are located and who you are in contact with. And this research on collective memory that we’ve pursued since we created Pantheon has tried to formalize these channels that influence what determines how famous someone will become.

**What are these channels?**

I say that collective memory has four Ts: technology, territory, tongue, and time. And we have published papers looking at how each one of them affects collective memory. Our newest paper on the power of localism is the culmination of a process in which we’re trying to understand each one of these forces and how it shapes who becomes famous and where and why and for how long and how big that fame can be.

**What you were saying about your experience with who seemed famous in Chile, does it run contrary to what you just found in your research about the importance of localism?**

No, I don’t think so. It’s all a patchwork of things in which you have these different forces working together. Let me walk you through some examples. We built this map of the influence of different languages based on the probability that a book has been translated between two of them. In that map, you can see that English is the global center of the world, while Spanish is a regional hub. French is also a regional language that connects to African language. Chinese is very big but it also connects to a few languages. Russian is a very important hub that connects to a lot of languages in Central Europe, Central Asia, and Eastern Europe, but it’s not a global hub.

If you look at the number of famous people associated with a particular language, you can think, well, maybe it’s because of populations in countries that speak that language, or maybe it’s because of wealth, or maybe it’s the way the languages are connected. But we find that the strongest correlation there is the centrality of a language in this network. What this tells you is that, if you make it big in English, all of the world is downstream from that fame.

If you make it big in a regional language, then you’re not going to have global fame until you go through one of these linguistic hubs and get to the rest of the world that way. So that was how tongue or how language shapes collective memory. And that was our first [paper](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5759bc7886db431d658b7d33/t/5783b68c9f74568e0024473b/1468249745815/PNAS-2014-Ronen-E5616-22.pdf), in _PNAS_ in 2014.

**What about technology, time and territory?**

Our second [paper](https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0205771) looked at the role of technology. If you look at the composition of collective memory, based on the number of famous people in an occupational category, it has changed over time, and those changes correspond to changes in technology. Before 1450, there are political and religious leaders. Then after the invention of printing, you get writers, you get painters, you get biologists, you get chemists. Then, once film is introduced, you switch from the people that write the art to the people that perform the art. It’s no longer the composer or the playwright. Now it’s the actor, the singer, the musician. And then with television, you know, you get the athlete. This paper confirms empirically this idea that the medium is the message.

The third T is time: That was a [paper](https://static1.squarespace.com/static/5759bc7886db431d658b7d33/t/5c1129b5c2241b7d0c8d672c/1544628763785/CandiaEtAl_NHB_2018.pdf) that we published in _Nature Human Behaviour_ in 2019. And it was motivated by this chart produced by a student of mine in which you see the date in which a song made it into the Billboard ranking as a function of how popular it is today in Spotify. With the rise to fame, you see a two step-process. The first part comes from people talking about things. The second part comes from people writing or using written records of what was talked about. When it comes to the decline, there are also two stages. Popularity doesn’t simply go down over time. It goes down with this sort of knee-shaped function, which is a fast decay and then a slow decay that comes later.

What we did in our newest [paper](https://academic.oup.com/pnasnexus/article/5/10/pgag308/8825253?searchresult=1&login=true) is focus on the idea of territory: Is there a local premium? Because in all of the papers that we looked at before, we look at how famous a person is and how that is shaped by the languages that people speak and how they are connected. We looked at how technology affects global fame as well. But we never separated between this local and this global component. We were always using this measure of aggregate attention. But attention is not all the same. Collective memories are more fragmented. Some memories are shared by certain groups of people very intensely, other memories maybe are shared globally, and other memories are shared by a lot of people just a little bit.

**Are you familiar with the idea of**[**sleeping beauties**](https://nautil.us/david-byrne-awakens-the-story-of-dark-matter-1285530)**, this theory written about by evolutionary biologist Andreas Wagner, that certain ideas from art and science can remain dormant, perhaps obscured by cultural biases and only emerge when the time is right?**

I don’t know if cultural bias is the only mechanism there, but I do know of examples of sleeping beauties that in some way involve ideas that sometimes are a bit ahead of their time and that take time to catch on. One example from my field that is relatively well known is chaos theory by Edward Lorenz.

Lorenz discovered in the early 1960s that a deterministic system could be unpredictable due to sensitivity to initial conditions. It was something that was extremely counterintuitive. He thought he was making a mistake on the calculation. It took him forever for him to accept that. And then chaos theory only became recognized about 10 or 20 years later as more people started to work on fluid dynamics and climate models.

The other example is the work of Mark Granovetter, a famous sociologist at Stanford who studied networks. He did this study in 1973 on how people got jobs. And he’s the one associated with the idea of the strength of weak ties. His work was well known within certain branches of sociology, and he founded the field of new economic sociology. But it really took off in the late ’90s and in the early 2000s when a lot of people started studying networks, you know, because of the rise of the web. A lot of people started to look at the structure of networks, whether networks had hubs or how clique-ish they were and all of that. And they encountered that literature. But until that moment, networks were more of a niche area of study.

**Do these sleeping beauties have different arcs in terms of how quickly they enter collective memory and fade?**

I wouldn’t be able to tell you that because we haven’t looked at that in particular. But what we have been able to look at, which is the paper that we have been working on, is this local premium. Here I have pictures of two characters. Do you know who the person on your left is?

**I believe that’s Napoleon.**

Yes, and maybe you recognize the picture of the person on the right.

**I don’t. I’m not sure who that is.**

That’s Bernardo O’Higgins.

**Oh, I should recognize him!**

Yes, Napoleon is globally famous, but it’s very easy to argue that in Chile, O’Higgins is as famous as Napoleon is in France. The main avenue in downtown Santiago is named after Bernardo O’Higgins. There are statues all over the country, and of course streets all over the country named after O’Higgins. There’s a university called Bernardo O’Higgins, movies about O’Higgins. There’s a region of the country called O’Higgins. There’s even a soccer team. He’s definitely very strong in our collective memory, but his fame is very localized. People in Chile, maybe a few people in Argentina or Peru, have heard of O’Higgins as one of the founding fathers of Latin America. But go to Indonesia, nobody has heard of O’Higgins—but they’ve heard of Napoleon. Fame can have this global and local component.

To measure this premium—how much of a person’s fame was local versus global—we had them play an online trivia game that is available in Pantheon, and we would ask people simple questions about a historical character. We had 41,000 players, about 400,000 answers, and about 10,000 players shared information with us about their country of origin, the language of origin, you know, their age and so forth. That was vital for us because we could use that to match people to the country of origin or the language of origin of the people that they answered questions about.

Let’s say you get a question about John Lennon. If you are from the U.K., he’s local twice in terms of language and in terms of country. If you are from Australia, he’s local once on language, but not on country. If you are French, he’s not local at all. We found that being from the same country gives you a nine percentage point advantage in knowing a particular figure. Speaking the same language gives you an additional four percentage points, so that’s 13 percentage points. Older people do much better here.

**Do some cultures excel at collective amnesia? Do they forget things more quickly?**

That goes into other things that I’ve worked on and researched, but there is very good evidence that as populations decrease in size, they lose the ability to produce technologies and they lose knowledge. One of the examples I can cite is that the population that moved into Tasmania over a land bridge [lost](https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/american-antiquity/article/abs/demography-and-cultural-evolution-how-adaptive-cultural-processes-can-produce-maladaptive-lossesthe-tasmanian-case/8CD08CC61E6FACF59EC02659B2BDA43C) bone tools, fishing and cold-weather clothing after the land bridge flooded. There are many examples also of seafaring populations who lose the ability to create the technologies that got them there because the islands could not support big enough populations.

**Are there benefits to the fading of memory or collective amnesia over time?**

Yes, there are benefits. The example that I use to illustrate the idea that sometimes forgetting can be beneficial is Project Chess from IBM. In the late ‘70s and early ‘80s, IBM was focused on the construction of big mainframe machines with these very ominous names. But the world was moving into personal computers that people could put on a desktop. Pivoting towards this smaller personal computer was going to be very hard for IBM, so there was an executive named Bill Lowe who decided to grab a group of engineers and relocate them out of Armonk and put them in Boca Raton in Florida.

He instructed them to develop a personal computer while forgetting everything that IBM was doing. It was this secret project, Project Chess, and they were able to come back to Armonk with a fully done solution that was the IBM personal computer. That was a way to use forgetting strategically, because sometimes to learn how to do something new you have to forget how to do what it is that you were doing before. But that’s in a very different context because we’re talking about productive knowledge, how to do things instead of this cultural collective memory.

**Do you think the idea transfers to larger cultural contexts?**

It might in some contexts in which the memory that you’re carrying can hold you back. I was in Rwanda for a UN mission on economic diversification and strategic development. Rwanda is a country that has a very difficult collective memory because of the genocide that took place there in the ’90s. But when you would talk to people, they would tell you this was something that had passed and they had been able to move past it. It was not something that defined their future, even though it was something that was part of their past.

There are a lot of countries that are much more hung up in their past conflicts. In Chile, we still suffer from the events of the 1970s and in Europe, there’s still a lot of memory from the Second World War and things that happened back then. At some point, the people of the future have to be liberated from the weight of their memories.

**Are there any other dimensions of collective memory that you want to investigate?**

One of the things that I’ve been wanting to do for a long time is to build an atlas of collective memory, much like my atlas of economic complexity. I’d love to put all of these collective memory ideas together in one big volume, that will help us understand the mechanisms that preserve and shape who it is that we remember, because I do believe that there’s a very romantic idea in collective memory.

It’s the idea that you see in movies like _Avatar_. The big thing that the Na’vi had was this ability to keep all of their memories in those trees that were connected to the center of the planet and so forth. As humans, we very much connect to that idea because what we have that makes us special is the fact that we are the recipients of a history of knowledge that is vast, that is useful, that is beautiful, that is inspired, and we get to live in a world of prosperity and possibilities because of that inherited knowledge.

To me, this collective memory agenda fits my larger body of work because what I’m really interested in understanding is not memory per se, but the mechanisms that govern the growth, diffusion, and value of knowledge. That’s the subject of my latest book, _The Infinite Alphabet_. Collective memory is just one chapter within the larger story. It’s a chapter that is important because it talks about the mechanisms of forgetting, but a lot of the work that I think is more interesting and more useful is the work that focuses on the mechanisms of learning.

Because at the end of the day, we want that knowledge to grow. Forgetting is what gnaws it away. But the mechanisms that help it grow are the ones that we need to help the developed world improve its levels of prosperity, its environmental conditions and so forth.

**With large language models now acting as a kind of repository for collective human culture and knowledge, is our relationship to collective memory going to change? Some evidence suggests AI is degrading our ability to learn or to think or to remember things.**

I don’t think so. It’s part of a continuum. It’s very similar to the conversation that the world had when the internet was introduced, and resources like Wikipedia. “All of the knowledge of the world now is available on Wikipedia!” But very few people went on to read it. We’ve been working on memory technologies for a long time—from the invention of language to the development of writing, to the invention of paper, to the invention of printing, to the invention of film and radio, to the invention of the telephone, television, the internet and the web. All of these are memory technologies.

For me, AI is another memory technology and probably in the future, the best way to know who I was and how I thought is gonna be to look at the logs of my conversations with these different AIs. I’m dedicating so much time to conversing with them right now—to get advice, to organize my agenda, what I need to do, what projects I need to work on. I do see it as a memory device, and I have no hangups uploading work that I’m doing to get feedback and everything like that. Because at the end of the day, if someone asks ChatGPT or Claude or Gemini about my book, I want the AI to give the most faithful possible answer. I’m not afraid of losing my copyright. I’m giving up on that. I’m an open-source type of guy.

I do see AI as a memory device, but at the same time, that ability to learn and to do great, I think it’s very much self-motivated and has always been. We have always had libraries full of books and very few people reading them. We have the internet with a lot of great content, and very few people using it to learn difficult things. Most people use it for entertainment. And now we have AI, and yes, a lot of people are using it to maybe avoid work and send long emails that they didn’t even read instead of putting in the effort to think. But some people are not.

My intuition is that the people who are using it properly and the people who are using it improperly have always been the same across all of these technological changes. It’s not that the technology shapes us, it’s that we have certain natural tendencies. Maybe 5 percent of the population is going to keep on learning and is going to get supercharged by AI. The other 95 percent was not learning with the previous technology either. That’s my cynical view. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The What and When of Longevity Dieting
content:
“Eat less to live longer” might be a good rule of thumb, but it’s horrible in practice. While animals living in laboratories may enjoy longer lives on calorie-restricted diets, humans living in the wild don’t enjoy starving themselves. To thread the needle, a new review [published](http://dx.doi.org/10.59717/j.xinn-nutri.2026.100034) in _Innovation Nutrition_ advances a longevity diet based on precision nutrition, with different recommendations for different ages.

Calorie restriction amounts to taking an axe to your diet, but this new approach argues for using a scalpel instead. Drawing on more than 30 longitudinal studies and meta-analyses of research on both humans and animals, the researchers sought to mimic the lifespan-boosting benefits of calorie restriction without the drawbacks. So they focused on finding the proper proportions and sources of macronutrients (protein, carbohydrates, fat, and fiber) to min-max the molecular mechanisms of our metabolisms.

**Read more: “**[**Longevity Research Has a Bullshit Problem**](https://nautil.us/longevity-research-has-a-bullshit-problem-1285933)**”**

The result is a dietary framework that changes with age. Take protein, for example. According to the team, eating more animal protein during midlife correlates with a higher mortality rate (but not for plant-based protein), but after age 65, the relationship flips. As risks from muscle loss and frailty increase during old age, our protein intake should ramp up to combat them. We should get that protein from fish, legumes, and other sources, the researchers say.

Macronutrients in recommendations for each age, percentages are based on total daily energy. “High evidence” means the findings come from multiple longitudinal studies and meta-analyses with mortality endpoints. “Moderate evidence” means the findings are supported primarily by proxy outcomes, like sarcopenia, frailty, and cardiometabolic biomarkers. _Credit: Huang J., Huang D. and Wu Z. (2026)_

Carbohydrates showed a J- or U-shaped relationship with mortality. The team found that risk of premature death was lowest in the middle of the graph, with 50 to 55 percent of the diet coming from carbs and emphasized that the source was important. Low-glycemic, plant-based, high-fiber carbohydrates from whole grains, legumes, vegetables, and whole fruits were much more conducive to a long life compared to refined grains and sugars.

The quality of fats was more important than the quantity, the researchers found. Polyunsaturated fats and monounsaturated fats from nuts, olive oil, and fish were linked to better cardiovascular health, while saturated and trans fats were linked to reduced mortality. One study found that swapping just 5 percent of energy from saturated fats to polyunsaturated fats was associated with a 25 to 42 percent reduction in coronary heart disease.

Fiber showed the most consistent link to longevity for all age groups. Our gut microbiome ferments fiber into short-chain fatty acids like butyrate that protect against creeping inflammation as we age. Altogether, higher fiber intake was associated with a 10 to 23 percent reduction in all-cause mortality, with fiber from plants and cereals showing the biggest gains.

Of course, your diet is a vital component of healthy aging and a longer life, but it’s not the only one. Proper sleep, exercise, and hydration are also important pieces of the longevity puzzle. To drive that point home, the team proposed their own “Dietary and Lifestyle Pyramid of Longevity” with these healthy practices providing a sturdy foundation.

The Dietary and Lifestyle Pyramid of Longevity, with food layers ordered by macronutrient quality rather than recommended frequency. _Credit: Huang J., Huang D. and Wu Z. (2026)_

The good news is that if we all follow it, we may live long enough to see a graphical representation of dietary recommendations in a shape that’s [not a pyramid](https://nautil.us/theres-a-new-international-food-pyramid-in-town-1286121). ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: Here’s Why It’s So Hard to Boost a Satellite
content:
NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last [look at the sky](https://theconversation.com/swifts-telescope-reveals-birth-deaths-and-collisions-of-stars-through-1-million-snapshots-in-uv-97044) on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about [171 miles (275 kilometers)](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/10/23/nasas-swift-mission-ends-ahead-of-re-entry/) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope’s mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn’t hold steady. The [telescope reentered the atmosphere on Nov. 4](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/11/02/nasas-swift-observatory-to-re-enter-atmosphere/) above the North Sumatra region of Indonesia and largely burned up, an abrupt ending to two decades spent [observing powerful cosmic explosions](https://theconversation.com/exploding-stars-send-out-powerful-bursts-of-energy-im-leading-a-citizen-scientist-project-to-classify-and-learn-about-these-bright-flashes-221294).

Swift’s reentry comes after a failed rescue mission in the summer of 2026. LINK, a commercial robotic spacecraft sent to raise Swift into a safer orbit, [reentered Earth’s atmosphere in September](https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/swift-rescue-mission-may-not-have-succeeded-but-no-regrets/). The machine designed to save a falling satellite burned up first.

[As a Ph.D. candidate in aerospace engineering](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=sx6X2OsAAAAJ&hl=en), I know that [rescuing satellites is hard](https://doi.org/10.64628/AAI.xdjcgwa97). [I research](https://doi.org/10.2514/6.2026-1921) how spacecraft approach and capture satellites, including objects that tumble uncontrollably.

Swift’s loss points to a new hazard for the young industry that repairs, refuels and moves spacecraft around in orbit. If something goes wrong, the spacecraft doing the rescuing can become another problem.

**The Rescuer Started Spinning**

The plan was for LINK to approach Swift, grab it with one of its three robotic arms and fire its thrusters to push the telescope back up to about [373 miles (600 kilometers)](https://spacepolicyonline.com/news/swift-reboost-mission-encounters-setback/) above Earth’s surface, where it could keep observing for years.

In late July, [LINK lost two of its three reaction wheels](https://www.space.com/space-exploration/missions/nasa-ends-swift-space-telescope-mission-after-failed-rescue-attempt), which are heavy wheels inside a spacecraft that help it turn without using fuel. That loss, combined with problems with its propulsion system, sent the spacecraft into an uncontrolled spin.

Without working wheels, a spacecraft steers with its thrusters instead, and every burn spends propellant.

Engineers eventually slowed LINK’s rotation by [firing its thrusters against the spin](https://gizmodo.com/nasas-plan-to-save-swift-just-got-a-software-fix-it-badly-needed-2000486000). NASA [reported in August](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/08/06/link-spacecraft-recovery-progressing-for-nasas-swift-boost/) that they had cut its spin from about nine degrees per second to roughly one and a half degrees per second.

Katalyst scientists stand with the LINK spacecraft in April 2026. It launched several months later, in July. _Credit: Sophia Roberts/NASA_

NASA and Katalyst Space, LINK’s builder, called off the capture and boost [later in August](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/09/04/commercial-spacecraft-for-nasas-swift-boost-continues-tech-demo/). The team still flew LINK within 7.5 to 9 miles (12 to 15 kilometers) of Swift, where it deployed LINK’s three robotic arms and tested its electric thrusters. It never got close enough to grab the telescope.

**Fuel Is the Rescue Budget**

A servicing spacecraft, like LINK, launches with a finite supply of propellant. Engineers split that fuel supply among the mission’s jobs, from reaching the target and approaching it safely to capturing it and moving it to a new orbit. They also pack some extra fuel in case of surprises.

Think of a tow truck that burns most of its gas getting itself out of a ditch. Even if it reaches a broken-down car, it may not have enough fuel left to tow it home.

That scenario is close to what happened to LINK. Even after engineers brought its spin under control, Katalyst said the spacecraft [no longer had enough propellant](https://www.cnn.com/2026/09/30/science/nasa-swift-observatory-falling) to capture Swift and raise its orbit safely.

A fuel budget that covers only the planned steps leaves nothing for recovering from a fault. But every extra pound of propellant also makes a spacecraft heavier, and heavier spacecraft cost more to launch and take more fuel to move.

**Speed Buys Time and Costs Backup**

Starting in 2024, [solar activity](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/10/23/nasas-swift-mission-ends-ahead-of-re-entry/) swelled Earth’s upper atmosphere, and the extra drag pulled Swift down faster than expected. Once NASA saw how quickly Swift was falling, the agency had to move fast to try to save the observatory. Space missions typically take years to develop and launch, but in this case, a slow, conventional development program risked arriving too late.

NASA awarded Katalyst a US$30 million contract in September 2025. The company had less than a year [to design, build, test and launch LINK](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/swift/swift-boost-mission/timeline/). LINK launched on July 3, 2026.

Speed comes with trade-offs. In engineering, a compressed schedule can leave less time for repeated testing, building spare hardware and planning recovery options. Public reports do not say whether that trade-off played any part in LINK’s faults.

[NASA has said](https://www.nasa.gov/news-release/nasa-updates-next-steps-for-commercial-swift-boost-mission/) that even though LINK didn’t succeed, the effort gave the agency experience in quickly building, launching and operating a servicing spacecraft. Engineers also showed they could [upload new control software](https://gizmodo.com/nasas-plan-to-save-swift-just-got-a-software-fix-it-badly-needed-2000486000) to steady a damaged servicing spacecraft with the hardware it had left. And LINK [tested its arms and fired all three thrusters at once](https://science.nasa.gov/blogs/swift/2026/09/04/commercial-spacecraft-for-nasas-swift-boost-continues-tech-demo/) in orbit.

**What Comes Next**

While Swift was the most pressing case for a boost mission, it’s not the only one. [NASA’s Hubble Space Telescope](https://science.nasa.gov/mission/hubble/) could one day use a similar boost, and [news reports suggested](https://www.azfamily.com/2026/08/20/nasa-telescope-doomed-after-flagstaff-companys-rescue-attempt-fails/) it would have been next in line had this mission worked.

Future missions are pursuing two complementary approaches for rescuing satellites. Astroscale’s [ELSA-M](https://www.space.com/astroscale-elsa-m-space-debris-removal-funding) is built to capture satellites that carry a docking plate installed before launch, which would make it easier for a rescuer to snag and boost them if the satellite eventually got into trouble. The European Space Agency’s [ClearSpace-1](https://www.esa.int/Space_Safety/ClearSpace-1) is planned for 2029 and aims to capture the Proba-1 satellite, which doesn’t have a docking plate or anything to help ClearSpace-1 capture it, and remove it from orbit.

LINK’s mission showed that a rescue takes more than a robotic arm and enough thrust to reach a target. It also takes a servicer spacecraft that can stay stable, recover from its own faults and keep enough propellant reserved to finish the job. In Swift’s case, the rescuer fell short before the rescue could begin. ![Image 1](https://lede-admin.nautil.us/wp-content/uploads/sites/70/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)![Image 2](https://assets.nautil.us/sites/3/nautilus/nautilus-favicon-14.png?fm=png)

title: The Evolving Story of How Chemistry Became Biology
content:
After decades of bickering about which molecules came first, a new generation of scientists is rethinking what life was, is, and could be.

[![Image 1](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/OOL-Badge.svg)](https://www.quantamagazine.org/a-new-era-for-the-dawn-of-life-20261112/)

A round 4.6 billion years ago, some 9 billion years after the birth of the universe, a cloud of gas and dust collapsed into the familiar blinding ball in our sky. Scraps of leftover material collided and accreted into the planets of the solar system, including our own. For the next few hundred million years, Earth was a hellish, molten landscape bombarded by meteorites. As it started to cool, water pooled into vast, acidic oceans. The days, half as long as today’s, passed under pink carbon dioxide skies. But life wasn’t around to sense any of it. Until it was.

Around 300 million years into the existence of our solar system, conditions on Earth were right for a great chemical experiment to begin. Molecules entangled themselves in self-sustaining, self-reproducing loops. Over time, these systems became more complex. At some point, they had come to life.

Life invented new ways to move, and to capture, store, and use energy. It began to sense, respond to, and change its environment. It communicated, ate some of its neighbors and lived inside others, and formed complex, dynamic communities. Through cycles of birth, reproduction, and death; catastrophe; and bursts of evolution, it persisted and then thrived, taking over every corner of the planet.

Then, at some point, life gained a sense of itself, a reflective intelligence with the existential curiosity to ask: Where did we come from? For tens of thousands of years, we have pondered and probed the origins of life: Monks have meditated, philosophers have argued, lovers have mused, and parents have patiently answered their kids’ questions.

“Go back in human history, go back to the Neanderthals, go back 30,000 years,” said [William Schopf (opens a new tab)](https://epss.ucla.edu/william-schopf/), a paleobiologist at the University of California, Los Angeles, “and one of the things you will see is that human beings have been wrestling with this question.”

By the mid-20th century, it became possible to probe life’s origins through chemistry, molecular biology, and genetics. Hypotheses exploded. Scientists clashed over which type of molecule — [RNA](https://www.quantamagazine.org/did-life-begin-in-an-rna-world-20261109/), [lipids](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-case-for-a-bubble-at-lifes-start-20261110/), [proteins](https://www.quantamagazine.org/peptides-on-stardust-may-have-provided-a-shortcut-to-life-20220308/), and [metabolites](https://www.quantamagazine.org/what-is-the-metabolism-first-theory-for-the-origin-of-life-20261111/) are prime suspects — could have started it all. The arguments have gone on for so long, without resolution or unifying insight, that some experts have considered the field to be in crisis.

“There’s nothing more exciting for a scientific field than a moment of crisis,” said [Betül Kaçar (opens a new tab)](https://www.kacarlab.org/), an astrobiologist and evolutionary biologist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison. “That’s when I think breakthroughs happen.”

![Image 2: A portrait of Betül Kaçar.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Betul_Kacar-cr.Sharon-Vanorny.webp)

Life’s origins are not purely a chemistry problem. “It’s not a linear reaction. … There’s no single _E_ = _mc_ 2 and that’s origin of life’s formula,” said Betül Kaçar, an astrobiologist and evolutionary biologist. “This is biology; it doesn’t follow any rules. That’s what makes it so sophisticated and exciting.”

Sharon Vanorny

A new wave of origins-of-life researchers, fed up with the tradition of bickering, have unshackled themselves from the idea that a single type of molecule started it all. Their open-minded approach has coincided with a change in scientific understanding. Experiments have shown that the precursors to many of life’s ingredients may have formed easily under the conditions on early Earth. What is harder to explain is how these molecular processes became a stable evolutionary system continuous with the vast diversity of life we see on the planet today. During life’s earliest days, these processes came together to store and pass on information, both consistently and imperfectly enough to allow the same living lineage to persist for billions of years on an ever-changing planet.

To study the emergence of lifelike biochemical systems, biologists are now pushing backward into the past from the living world with new genetic tricks, while chemists are pushing forward from the nonliving world with new and strange mixtures of molecules. And by combining tools from chemistry and biology, synthetic biologists are embracing informed speculation and probing novel biological systems that may not have ever existed. Scientists now engaged with the origins of life are asking not just what life is, but what it does — on an archaic world, in a lab dish, or somewhere beyond our atmosphere.

## **The Origins**

In 1952, [Stanley Miller (opens a new tab)](https://www.nasonline.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/06/miller-stanley.pdf), then a graduate student at the University of Chicago, performed a bold experiment. He was inspired by a lecture⁠ given by [Harold Urey (opens a new tab)](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1934/urey/biographical/), the Nobel Prize–winning chemist, on the origins of the solar system. In the 1920s, Alexander Oparin in Russia and J.B.S. Haldane in England had independently hypothesized that life gradually evolved from a “primordial soup” of molecules. Urey proposed an extension of that idea: that Earth’s primitive atmosphere was composed of gases that could, with a little help from an energy source like lightning, produce organic molecules that would rain into the ocean. From there, these molecules would accumulate, concentrate, and eventually start to link together on the way to self-replication.

A year after hearing the lecture, Miller, just 23 at the time, approached Urey with a proposal. A week later, he had scraped together what would become known as the Miller-Urey apparatus: A glass bulb filled with water simulated a primordial ocean, and a second filled with gases (methane, ammonia, water vapor, and hydrogen) approximated a primordial atmosphere. A candle heated the water, and electrodes created sparks in the gas. The “atmosphere” was then run through a condenser that cooled it into liquid “rain” that fell into the “ocean.”

The next day, a dark brown sludge had formed at the bottom of the bulb. It contained five different types of amino acids, the small molecules that link up to form proteins, the workhorses of cells. Miller had shown that life’s building blocks could form in the conditions of early Earth, as they were understood at the time.

“It was paradigm-shifting,” said [Ramanarayanan Krishnamurthy (opens a new tab)](https://www.scripps.edu/faculty/krishnamurthy/), an organic chemist at Scripps Research. “It really changed the field and gave rise to what we call prebiotic chemistry.”

“This is the first experiment in the field showing that these deep questions on the origins of life were not only the realm of metaphysics, philosophy, and religion,” said [Christophe Danelon (opens a new tab)](https://www.toulouse-biotechnology-institute.fr/en/christophe-danelon/), a synthetic biologist at the Toulouse Biotechnology Institute in France.

![Image 3: Stanley Miller in 1953 stands in front of a chemistry setup.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Stanley-Miller-cr.Bettmann-Gettyimagesjpg-copy.webp)

![Image 4: Two round flasks are connected by pipes; it’s the Miller -Urey apparatus.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Stanley-Miller-Aparatus-cr.Stanley-Miller.webp)

In the early 1950s, Stanley Miller (top) performed a foundational experiment in the study of the origins of life. By simulating an early Earth environment inside a glass apparatus (bottom), he was able to form the precursors of amino acids.

Bettmann/Getty Images; Stanley Miller

In the early 1950s, Stanley Miller (left) performed a foundational experiment in the study of the origins of life. By simulating an early Earth environment inside a glass apparatus (right), he was able to form amino acids.

Bettmann/Getty Images; Stanley Miller

At first, life’s origin was largely considered a chemistry problem. But biology soon played the role of muse. In 1953, just a few weeks before Miller [published his famous experiment (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.117.3046.528), the biologists Francis Crick and James Watson published [the helical structure of DNA (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0).

The realization that DNA was central to all life suggested that genetic molecules were probably critical to life’s origin, too. The field shifted to explaining genetics, said [David Baum (opens a new tab)](https://baumlab.botany.wisc.edu/current-lab-members/), an evolutionary biologist at the University of Wisconsin, Madison.“We became so obsessed.”

The molecular biology revolution further clarified the most fundamental characteristics of cells: a genome to store information, a metabolism to provide energy, and a compartment to hold it all together. The materials of life became the field’s focus; if they just found the right starting molecule, the thinking went, everything else, including self-replication and evolution, would swiftly follow.

This period also marked the beginning of the dustups that would characterize the field for decades.

“The first thing that people then chose to do was to pick one of life’s molecules and assume that was the progenitor, the kind of ‘first molecule,’ and all of the others could temporarily be ignored,” said [Matthew Powner (opens a new tab)](https://pownerlab.com/matthewpowner.html), a chemist at University College London. “The absolute classic version of this was the RNA-world theory.”

The [RNA-world theory](https://www.quantamagazine.org/did-life-begin-in-an-rna-world-20261109/), the most popular and well-studied theory of life’s origin, came together following a critical discovery. RNA is a single molecular strand that copies genetic information from DNA’s double strands, which the cell then reads and translates into proteins using complex, highly evolved enzyme molecules. In the 1980s, the scientists Thomas Cech and Sidney Altman independently discovered that some RNA molecules also act as enzymes that catalyze, or activate, biochemical reactions; this research [won them a Nobel Prize (opens a new tab)](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/chemistry/1989/summary/). RNA therefore offered a tantalizing solution to how early life could have both stored information and replicated itself without the enzymes it uses today: RNA could, in theory, do it all.

The RNA-first theory wasn’t the only option that emerged. In the 1970s, the discovery of hydrothermal vents in the Pacific, along with the strange creatures that call them home, roused the field once more. In 1988, Günter Wächtershäuser, a German patent lawyer with a doctorate in chemistry, [proposed an “iron-sulfur” world (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1016/S0723-2020(88)80001-8), suggesting that iron-sulfide minerals that collect near hydrothermal vents could have kick-started primitive versions of metabolism. Around the same time, the complexity theorist [Stuart Kauffman (opens a new tab)](https://www.kli.ac.at/en/people/kli_external_faculty/view/227), now an emeritus professor of biochemistry at the University of Pennsylvania, popularized theories on “autocatalytic sets,” molecular chain reactions in which one molecule catalyzes the next, which catalyzes the next, and so on in a circular process. These ideas fueled the theory of [a metabolism-first world](https://www.quantamagazine.org/what-is-the-metabolism-first-theory-for-the-origin-of-life-20261111/), which proposes that life arose as self-sustaining networks of molecules interacting and indefinitely making more of each other. In this world, the storage of genetic information would come later.

Though the RNA world and metabolism-first world were often pitted against each other, there were other contenders. There was also [a lipid world](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-case-for-a-bubble-at-lifes-start-20261110/), in which the molecules that form cell membranes and contain cellular chemistry came first. There was a protein or peptide world, a virus world, a coenzyme world, a zinc world, and even a clay world. “You can find any world you ever imagined predicated on whatever your background was when you joined this field,” Powner said.

The scientists also debated _where_ life started. Did it evolve in “warm little ponds,” as Darwin proposed more than a century ago, or in the oceans, in patches of ice at the poles, or at hydrothermal vents? Some molecular theories were coupled to specific environments, while others could have started in many places. Each approach had its staunch supporters.

“These were often presented as complete hypotheses that could explain the origin of life to the exclusion of the others,” said [Aaron Goldman (opens a new tab)](https://www.oberlin.edu/aaron-goldman), an evolutionary biologist at Oberlin College.

And that meant that only one hypothesis could be right.

## **The Crisis**

Throughout the early 2000s, conferences that focused on the origins of life were like arenas. Researchers argued in public, talked over one another, and even got into shouting matches. “It was unbelievable bickering,” said [Michael Travisano (opens a new tab)](https://cbs.umn.edu/directory/michael-travisano), an evolutionary biologist at the University of Minnesota.

“There used to be open fights,” Krishnamurthy said.

Some professors forbade their students to discuss ideas with other labs. They even dissed each other in the press. In 1992, _Discover_ magazine reported that Miller, a prebiotic-soup proponent, didn’t want to even discuss the vent hypothesis and thought of it as “a real loser.”

Science is no stranger to arguments, but the rifts in the origins field went particularly deep. That was due in part to its multidisciplinary nature. Origins-of-life researchers are chemists, biologists, geologists, physicists, and everything in between. They receive different types of training, use different definitions, and subscribe to different worldviews.

“Arguments were difficult to resolve because everybody was making a good point,” said [John Sutherland (opens a new tab)](https://mrclmb.ac.uk/research-leaders/john-sutherland/), an organic chemist at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in the United Kingdom. “Yes, you do need RNA. Yes, you do need peptides. Yes, you do need metabolites.”

Plus, absent a time machine, there is no way to prove or falsify any hypothesis. Scientists have minimal direct evidence. “You can hold on to your theory forever, and nobody will ever really be able to say you are absolutely wrong,” said [Elisa Biondi (opens a new tab)](https://blueplanetred.net/elisa-biondi), a geneticist at the Foundation for Applied Molecular Evolution.

Experiments were little help, as efforts to create something resembling life from a single kind of molecule were not fruitful. Researchers haven’t been able to get an RNA molecule to self-replicate, nor have they compelled an autocatalytic metabolic network to sustain itself, grow, and pass down information. The proposed locations — hydrothermal vents, shallow pools, ice caps — also couldn’t support on their own the chemistry that seemed necessary to get life going.

“When people first started studying the origin of life, the perspective was we just need the really good idea that will solve [it],” Goldman said. “That way of pursuing the question turned out to not work.”

Decades of evidence from experiments further challenged the idea that a single molecule or environment could have kick-started life on its own. Prebiotic chemistry experiments not only yielded scores of amino acids, but also created sugars, nucleobases, and fatty acids — the building blocks of proteins, RNA, DNA, and lipids — and their precursors. And [detailed analysis of samples](https://www.quantamagazine.org/the-cosmos-teems-with-complex-organic-molecules-20241113/) that arrived on Earth from space uncovered an array of organic materials. Meteorites such as Murchison, which fell in Australia in 1969, and Murray, which exploded over Kentucky in 1950, carried a diversity of amino acids and some nucleobases.

![Image 5: Portrait of Aaron Goldman.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Aaron-Goldman-cr.Sara-Verosky.webp)

How life began is a “difficult question that is just on the edge of scientifically tractable,” said Aaron Goldman, an evolutionary biologist. “Saying we’re going to solve it is kind of like saying we’re going to solve medicine.”

Sara Verosky

By the early 2010s, it was becoming clearer that the creation of life’s starting materials wasn’t that difficult. “It struck me,” Sutherland said, “that maybe where [we’re] wrong is this assumption that you couldn’t have chemistry that makes everything.”

This revelation shifted the field’s focus from identifying the singular molecule or process that started life to understanding how a more general prebiotic chemistry could have formed — a true primordial, biochemical soup. The individual worlds expanded to include the possibility of multiple types of molecules. However, only a subset would go on to be preserved as the building blocks of biology.

The thinking used to be “How do we make anything?” said [Cole Mathis (opens a new tab)](https://search.asu.edu/profile/1475259), an astrobiologist at Arizona State University. Now, it’s “How do we not make everything?”

The process of generating many types of biomolecules in sufficient volumes could have been iterative and long, spanning perhaps hundreds of thousands or even millions of years. These materials would have had to accumulate in a contained area, whether that was a pond, a shallow sea, a vent, or all of the above, and not be washed away or otherwise degraded by time.

![Image 6: A colorful turquoise pool billows steam. It is surrounded by red soil and tourists.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Prismatic-Spring-cr.Ted-Kinsman_ScienceSource-scaled.webp)

Scientists have proposed energetic, mineral-rich hot springs, such as the Grand Prismatic Spring in Yellowstone National Park, as environments where life may have begun.

Ted Kinsman/Science Source

Building up that initial molecular pool is “what could be really, really hard, really rare” in the universe, said [Jack Szostak (opens a new tab)](https://chemistry.uchicago.edu/jack-w-szostak), a [Nobel Prize–winning (opens a new tab)](https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/medicine/2009/szostak/facts/) origins-of-life researcher at the University of Chicago. “Going from environment to environment, from reservoir to reservoir, to actually an environment where protocells can form … maybe that’s just astronomically rare.”

If an initial, diverse molecular pool was the most important condition, then fighting over separate worlds is a waste of breath. Many researchers today, especially early- and mid-career researchers frustrated by the infighting, are eager for new, better ideas. They’re meeting up at formal and informal workshops and meetings to build bridges between different fields pursuing the same questions instead of letting disciplinary differences calcify into battle lines. “We are now at a point where we realize, well, maybe it’s not that my world is better than your world, but they have to coexist,” Kaçar said.

The general attitude among these mostly younger folks is “if you don’t do it, we’ll do it,” said [Joana Xavier (opens a new tab)](https://jcxavier.org/), who in 2020 as a postdoc co-founded the [Origin of Life Early-Career Network (opens a new tab)](https://www.oolen.org/) with Mathis. She is currently meditating on her time in the field at a Buddhist monastery in southern France.

Compared to their scientific predecessors, this group of researchers is “less imperialistic about our specific science,” said [Ludo Schoenmakers (opens a new tab)](https://ludoschoenmakers.nl/), a postdoc in philosophy of science at KU Leuven in Belgium. “I guess we don’t think that it automatically ranges over all of reality.”

Joana Xavier sits at the Nalanda Monastery in France. When she’s not meditating, the researcher on hiatus is writing the story of the origins of life. “My issue is, I keep navigating between extremely complex mathematical stuff and almost poetry,” she said.

Nalanda Monastery, France

This moment in research into the origins of life is intellectually diverse and open to new possibilities. Researchers are eager to think beyond single molecules or settings and instead investigate complex networks and systems made of many molecules. They’re thinking about how evolution could have emerged from this mess. And many have stopped thinking that it had to be some singular occurrence. Hydrothermal vents or warm ponds? “Why not both?” said [Joanna Masel (opens a new tab)](https://www.masellab.org/), an evolutionary biologist at the University of Arizona. “I believe that there were multiple origins of life.”

When life takes hold, a system of interacting molecules “frees itself from where it was born,” Krishnamurthy said. Origins researchers have done the same. The field is finding new ways to ask and answer parts of the vast question by collaborating across disciplines. They are turning to bold new experiments and creative ideas that expand our understanding of what life is and what it could be.

As the biochemist [Gerald Joyce (opens a new tab)](https://www.salk.edu/scientist/gerald-joyce/), the president of the Salk Institute who led research into the RNA world, put it: “Let a thousand flowers bloom.”

## **The Progenitor**

One way to approach how life started is to think like the chemists: Start with nonliving molecules and bring them to life. Another way is to think like an evolutionary biologist: Trace life backward to its most ancient root, and perhaps beyond.

If you were to take everything that’s alive today — from blooming flowers and trees to humans and dogs to single cells encrusting a hydrothermal vent — and trace every lineage back through billions of years, you’d eventually reach a single point. This cell, from which all life known to us has descended, is the root of the tree of life.

In the 1990s, this cell (or, more accurately, this population of cells) got a name: the “last universal common ancestor,” or LUCA. [Biologists debated (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1542973) who or what LUCA was: whether it resembled a modern cell or was something simpler. LUCA left no fossils — the oldest uncontested ancient fossils date to around 3.5 billion years ago — but it has left a different material record from billions of years ago.

“There are only two records of past life,” said [Greg Fournier (opens a new tab)](https://eaps.mit.edu/people/faculty/gregory-fournier/), an evolutionary biologist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. One is dead remains of ancient organisms fossilized in the rock record. The second, he said, is “the record within genomes … traces that have been passed down from the first cells to all life or almost all life alive today.”

![Image 8: Greg Fournier sits on stones in a field.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Greg-Fournier-cr.Courtesy-of-Greg-Fournier.webp)

“We’re trying to understand meaningful, important things about our place in the universe,” said Greg Fournier, an evolutionary biologist. “It’s equivalent to trying to find the Higgs boson, or trying to come up with a theory of quantum gravity, or trying to understand the Big Bang.”

Courtesy of Greg Fournier

By the early 2000s, the genomic era was in full swing, and over the following decades sequencing technologies got better and faster. Today, “we can sequence entire genomes containing thousands of genes in under an hour,” Fournier said. Complete genomes of species from across the tree of life started piling up. By comparing them, the biologists who build trees of life, known as phylogeneticists, could map out their evolutionary relationships.

The logic of building phylogenetic trees is straightforward: Compare the genomes of distantly related species— say, a bacterium and a human — to reveal potentially shared genes that may have evolved before those lineages split. To tell LUCA’s story, researchers identify the most ancient genes that are found in all modern living things.

LUCA’s story is regularly rewritten and refined based on new genetic clues as well as advances in scientific understanding. For example, bacteria often pass genes to their neighbors, or across bacterial species, in an evolutionary process known as horizontal gene transfer. Once biologists realized that these signals can [wrongly suggest](https://www.quantamagazine.org/chronological-clues-to-lifes-early-history-lurk-in-gene-transfers-20180424/) that certain genes have a shared evolutionary history, they had to find better ways to interpret their vast dataset. The computational techniques to do so finally arrived in the last decade. In 2024, a research group led by [Phil Donoghue (opens a new tab)](https://www.bristol.ac.uk/people/person/Philip-Donoghue-4fd2d6ef-3986-4566-97e4-7ae7db296525/) at the University of Bristol used some of these techniques in novel ways to paint the richest picture of LUCA yet.

![Image 9: Small boulders sit in shallow water. They are stromatolites.](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Stromatolites-cr.B-G-Thomson-ScienceSource-scaled.webp)

These boulderlike stromatolites from Shark Bay, Australia, are layered structures built by microorganisms. Not far away, in Pilbara in western Australia, are fossil stromatolites dating back to 3.48 billion years ago — some of the oldest fossils known on the planet.

B.G. Thomson/Science Source

They reported that LUCA likely operated [with around 2,600 proteins (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41559-024-02461-1) encoded by a genome comparable in size to those in modern-day bacteria. Those genes and proteins suggested that LUCA had a basic metabolism, a functional cell membrane, and even a primitive immune system for fighting viruses. It had all the basic equipment for making energy, replicating DNA, and producing proteins. Altogether, the analysis painted a picture of an already complex organism.

“LUCA was a fully flesh, swimming, eating, reproducing, messy cell,” Kaçar said. And wherever it lived, it likely didn’t live alone.

Donoghue’s team found that LUCA had a metabolic pathway that is nearly identical to one found in modern microbes, known as the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway. Intriguingly, this metabolic pathway is related to another metabolic process, acetogenesis, that cannot work on its own but relies on the processes of other cells: LUCA’s neighbors. This makes it very likely that LUCA was part of a larger community or ecosystem containing multiple types of early cells.

Donoghue’s team also estimated an age for LUCA’s lineage: 4.2 billion years old. Given that the planet is thought to have cooled enough to become habitable around 4.4 billion years ago, LUCA’s community must have evolved in the blink of an evolutionary eye. “Life gets going pretty fast when the conditions are favorable,” Masel said.

If LUCA was already a complex population and included many types of cells, then a meaningful portion of life’s early evolutionary history must have occurred well before it lived. By then, the available molecular and cellular diversity must have gone far beyond the basic rudiments of life; it was enough for evolutionary processes to have selected for complex molecular machines and systems.

This revelation has compelled some biologists, who by definition study life forms that evolved after LUCA, to shift their target to the life forms, quasi-life forms, and lifelike processes that may have existed before LUCA. They’re using new tools to push beyond the material record’s limits to predict how this cellular ecosystem might have evolved in the prebiotic soup.

“What was happening before LUCA really is the most exciting window to look at,” said [Klára Hlouchová (opens a new tab)](https://khlab.org/), a synthetic biologist at Charles University in Prague. It’s also “the hardest one to pin down.” To do that, researchers are getting imaginative about the chemistries that could have emerged in this early window and rapidly led to evolutionary innovations.

## **The Possibilities**

Among the genes that we believe comprised LUCA are some that clearly have a more ancient origin. These genes are so old that nearly all genomes across the tree of life have not only one copy of them, but two. This points to an evolutionary event — [a DNA duplication](https://www.quantamagazine.org/genome-duplication-is-a-radical-evolutionary-gamble-20260902/) — that occurred well before LUCA evolved. Such genes can take biologists further back and closer to life’s origins.

“They’re a way to look at what life was like even before the earliest organism,” Goldman said. The protein products made by these doubled genes are involved in [a modern cell’s most fundamental processes (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xgen.2026.101140), such as making proteins, transporting molecules across a membrane, and metabolizing molecules into energy.

Goldman is particularly interested in the latter two. Most life on Earth uses a series of molecular pumps, known as an electron transport chain, to generate energy to power cells. By tracing back the phylogenies of the molecules involved in modern electron transport chains, Goldman proposes what prebiotic, pre-LUCA versions of these molecules might have looked like.

Then [Laurie Barge (opens a new tab)](https://science.jpl.nasa.gov/people/barge/), an astrobiologist at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, tests how these plausibly ancient molecules might have behaved in prebiotic environments. Goldman, an evolutionary biologist, met Barge in 2009 at an astrobiology conference for graduate students in Seattle. “We met and became friends there, and we’re in totally different fields,” Barge said. “We had nothing in common … and we grew up together.” Now they collaborate to bring evolutionary biology and prebiotic chemistry together.
