In glass jars on their lab bench, Barge and her colleague [Jessica Weber (opens a new tab)](https://science.jpl.nasa.gov/people/weber/), also a NASA JPL chemist, simulate the possible mineral chemistries of hydrothermal chimneys — ones that may have been present on primordial Earth as well as those that might exist elsewhere in the universe. They synthesize minerals from their chimney experiments and mix them in vials with Goldman’s pre-LUCA molecules, and test [whether and how they interact (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2210924120) to produce chemistry reminiscent of an electron transport chain.

Barge and Weber are building from the bottom up to determine what is prebiotically plausible, while Goldman is going from the top down, making predictions from modern and historical clues. They may meet at a fundamental process right in the gray area between life and nonlife. “We come at the problem from two different directions,” Barge said. “Combining the two is powerful since then we can study prebiotic plausibility and evolutionary continuity at the same time.”

Even if they succeed in producing aspects of a prebiotic electron transport chain, there’s no assurance that this is how this important metabolic system arose. The deeper scientists reach into pre-LUCA time, the fuzzier the picture becomes. “Still, it is important to understand the prebiotic possibilities,” Barge said.

The time period before LUCA is so fuzzy that we don’t even know if life then was built using the same ingredients that life uses today. After billions of years of evolution, modern biology could have changed significantly. Evolution is not a designer; the systems that stuck were those that worked, not necessarily the optimal ones for the job. Plus, early organisms led a very different life in a very different environment more than 4 billion years ago; different materials may have been available or may have worked more effectively there.

These deep uncertainties about early evolution on Earth naturally pose questions about how life could evolve anywhere across the universe. As a child, Hlouchová would lay awake at night after watching alien movies, terrified at the question: Is there life out there? When she grew up, she started asking a different version of it: Could life emerge from other chemistries?

At her lab down the street from Prague’s medieval astronomical clock, she deconstructs the amino acid alphabet, which guides the structure and function of all life on Earth. The hundreds of millions of types of proteins found across nature are all built from the same 20 amino acids. But dozens of other types of amino acids have been found on meteorites. It’s possible to make thousands more in the lab, and scientists have speculated that there could be millions of variants across the universe. The rise of more powerful artificial intelligence systems and synthetic biology tools has equipped biologists such as Hlouchová to design molecules, produce them, and test them in the lab.

![Image 14](https://www.quantamagazine.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Klara-Hlouchova-cr.Matej-Hlouch.webp)

“This [the origins of life] is something we should crack as humankind,” said Klára Hlouchová, a synthetic biologist. “This problem really opens up our eyes to the rest of the universe.”

Matej Hlouch

Maybe, during life’s pre-LUCA years, proteins were built with more or fewer amino acids, or even with a totally different set. “Computationally, we think that yes — life could have used different amino acids,” Hlouchová said. “We know that our amino acids were easily available, at least the half of them, and they would be very accessible to prebiotic synthesis on planets which would be similar to ours.” And on a different planet, with different chemistry, she said, “you could have different amino acids and … you could eventually build life using different ways.”

To test these ideas, Hlouchová is now building proteins in the lab using a reduced amino acid alphabet. Rather than focus on a specific ancient protein, as Goldman and Barge are doing, she’s looking at three specific types of folding structures found in many types of proteins — folds produced when an amino acid sequence bends and stretches into a 3D shape — that are known to be highly conserved across known life and thus very ancient in origin.

Using a combination of [protein-design and structure-prediction](https://www.quantamagazine.org/how-ai-revolutionized-protein-science-but-didnt-end-it-20240626/) programs, her lab removed the modern amino acid alphabet from the protein fold’s 3D structure. Then they asked the program to repopulate it using a reduced alphabet. Using a generative AI tool trained on large sets of protein folds, the programs predicted sequences that would fold up into the desired structure. Hlouchová then built the most plausible ancient proteins and imaged them.

Her team reported, in [a series of recent studies (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.tibs.2026.08.002), that a reduced alphabet of just 10 amino acids could support the kinds of protein structures that were likely found early in life’s development, the most robust protein folds that modern life uses. She is now working on repeating these experiments with totally different amino acids.

Using biology as a guide, and chemical possibilities as a parts list, Hlouchová is probing what life may have looked like before LUCA.

Synthetic biology “opens up a whole new world where we just don’t have to rely on life that we see today,” Hlouchová said. “Did life have to happen this way, or could it have happened in different ways?” Answering the question could mean traveling ever farther away from what we might recognize as biology.

## **The Processes**

From the start, modern life has inspired the study of life’s origins. Miller considered his experiment’s production of amino acids, a core feature of modern life, to be irrefutable evidence that life could be produced from early Earth chemistry. And more recent researchers use today’s most widespread biomolecules and processes as proxies for features early life must have had. But researchers hold varying opinions on whether, and how much, we should allow modern life to constrain our imaginations.

“It would be foolish to ignore life as a guide,” Krishnamurthy said, “but it would be even more foolish to use life as the only guide.”

Instead of focusing on the exact materials of life, some are trying to re-create its essence. The field has “been too focused on what molecules current life works with,” said [Sijbren Otto (opens a new tab)](https://otto-lab.com/home/sijbren-otto/), a systems chemist at the University of Groningen. It has “not looked enough at what life does.”

Life is made up of not only molecules but functions. It can replicate, it can metabolize, and it can evolve. These functions don’t necessarily need to be performed by the same molecules that life uses today.

For example, could another molecular system do what DNA does? “If you generalize the definition of a gene, you say, ‘OK, it’s a molecule that stores information,’” Otto said. A replication process generates copies of that information. While Hlouchová is looking at whether you can get to the same structure with different molecules, Otto is looking at whether you can get to the same function. In the early 2010s, he started testing whether nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA, are the only molecules that can store and pass on information.

[Benzene rings (opens a new tab)](https://www.chem.ucla.edu/~harding/IGOC/B/benzene_ring.html) are stable structures made of interlocking rings of carbon and hydrogen that are found in many biological molecules, including several amino acids. By chance, in 2010, Otto discovered that certain types of synthetically made benzene rings of the same size tended to stack neatly, like poker chips. When shaken or stirred, the growing stacks broke, which triggered the molecular edges to grow more benzene rings. This was [a kind of self-replication (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1182767).

The stacks of benzene rings were also, in essence, propagating information: the size of the rings. The new stacks, which Otto found could just keep growing, always contained rings of the same size. “From that moment on, we realized we stand a chance of doing evolution with these types of systems,” he said.

These chemical structures held the possibility of information storage and replication. The next step would be to induce metabolism, or to get the structures to facilitate other chemical reactions. They would also need a container to hold themselves together. Putting it all together was a dream, but one that’s gotten closer than ever in recent years.

It took Otto’s lab another 10 years to figure out how to get their self-replicating molecules to [catalyze reactions (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41929-020-0463-8) other than their own replication, such as those that helped them make their own precursors. Then, in still unpublished work, they altered some of the molecules in a way that compelled the rings to form compartments that grew and divided. “It’s replicating, it’s metabolizing, it’s keeping itself together in a compartment,” Otto said. Eventually the “benzene cells” grew big enough to be seen under a microscope, he said.

But does that make them alive? The only thing they’re really missing, from a functional perspective, is the ability to evolve, Otto said. That’s [where his lab is headed (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41557-023-01301-2) next. “We’re trying to make something that starts to approach life,” he said. “But it will be on a life support machine for some time to come.”

His benzene “cells” are a far cry from life as we know it. But if you can figure out conceptually how evolution could arise, Otto argued, you can reenact that mechanism, under the simulated conditions of the early Earth and with your favorite prebiotic molecules. “I think, then, you’re closer to the origin,” Otto said.

These scientists and others are probing the most fundamental aspects of life unhindered by the evolutionary journey that led from LUCA to today. They’re going beyond what genomics can tell us even about the pre-LUCA era to imaginatively reconstruct how the mechanisms and functions of life could have emerged. Despite their different tools, materials, and approaches, the common thread across the field is preserving the requirements and possibilities of evolution. Because no matter what molecules it’s built of, what makes life _alive_ is the fact that it can adapt to a changing environment and invent new ways to survive across deep time. Its engine of change and adaptation is evolution — and re-creating it is the shared dream of chemists and biologists alike.

## **The Continuum**

In summer 2026, [a cell](https://www.quantamagazine.org/for-the-first-time-a-cell-built-from-scratch-grows-and-divides-20260701/) made headlines. Synthetic biologists had packed fatty sacs called liposomes with biological components: a DNA replication system and a set of 36 enzymes that read DNA and make proteins. They filled other liposomes with sugar, lipids, enzymes, nucleotides, and ribosomes — supply caches to send in as needed. Then they waited to see if their chemistry experiment would take on a life of its own.

After months of fussing around with a population of these proto-cells in the lab, the team started to see something: lifelike behaviors. The cells replicated their DNA, grew, and divided. And larger ones produced more daughter cells, resulting in a crude kind of natural selection. The researchers posted [their results (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.07.01.735724)on the preprint server biorxiv.org in July. It was touted as a “[stunning (opens a new tab)](https://www.science.org/content/article/lab-created-spudcell-marks-major-step-toward-building-life-scratch)” step and a “[breakthrough (opens a new tab)](https://www.discovermagazine.com/world-s-first-synthetic-cell-with-a-complete-life-cycle-marks-biology-breakthrough-49331)” for the field.

This synthetic cell is not a reflection of the origin of life; it had a 4-billion-year head start. It was built from biomolecular parts that are highly evolved and “disgustingly modern,” said [Kate Adamala (opens a new tab)](https://cbs.umn.edu/directory/kate-adamala), the synthetic biologist at the University of Minnesota who led the project. But it’s the first plausible demonstration of the field’s most fundamental idea: that it is possible to take a bunch of “undeniably dead” components, she said, put them together, and create something that “starts undergoing all of those functions of life.”

Even though the cells can grow, divide, and replicate their genome, Adamala is steering clear of the word “alive.” The cell can’t feed and sustain itself; it needs constant delivery of food and ribosomes, the machinery that it needs to make proteins. But more importantly, Adamala said, it is missing true evolution.

To produce their crude version of natural selection, Adamala’s team engineered mutations into their synthetic cells that led to different growth rates. “It’s a poor man’s evolution,” she said. In true natural selection, cells would mutate, and the population would naturally gain genetic diversity. Her team had effectively built evolution in.

But still, the chemistry came together into something like biology. And it did not require some magic spark or special ingredient. The researchers had to figure out the molecular system — the relationships between known components — and then tweak them until the system worked better, and then better, and then better. Life is not an on-off-switch; it is more like a continuum. A chemical system becomes increasingly alive over time. And if you try to trace it back to a point at which it fully becomes alive, that point will likely be “arbitrary,” Otto said. This is true in the lab, and it must have been true 4 billion years ago.

To this day, no one has convincingly re-created life — self-sustaining, self-replicating, independently evolving — in the lab. Researchers aren’t even sure whether evolutionary processes on the early Earth, in systems of molecules that may or may not have been “alive,” would look like those that drive adaptive changes in cells or organisms today.

But give the scientists a little more time to work on the problem. “Our great chemists, only a handful of them, are doing this in the lab, and with only a few test tubes over a [a few] decades,” said [Michael Lynch (opens a new tab)](https://search.asu.edu/profile/3175331), an evolutionary biologist at Arizona State University who is working with Kaçar, Travisano, and others to [bring evolutionary rules (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2605.05464) to the origins-of-life field. In comparison, prebiotic chemistry on early Earth had a few hundred million years, which is “an awful long time for life to experiment.”

Similar experiments could be taking place somewhere out there right now. Our galaxy alone has at least 6,000 known exoplanets and likely many, many more. A lot of them have liquid water, and some 2,000 of them could be [super-Earths (opens a new tab)](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/10/13/science/inhabitable-planets-solar-system.html), even more hospitable to life than our own planet. Ancient [Mars](https://www.quantamagazine.org/its-raining-mars-interview-with-meteor-scientist-meenakshi-wadhwa-20181218/) and [Enceladus](https://www.quantamagazine.org/icy-oceans-exist-on-far-off-moons-why-arent-they-frozen-solid-20231102/), a moon of Saturn, support the conditions that astrobiologists consider necessary for life. Analyses of rock samples from [asteroids (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41561-025-01838-6) and [the red planet (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-70656-0) continue to reveal the raw materials used by our biology.

As researchers continue to deconstruct and reconstruct what life could have been on early Earth, they’re also exploring what could be possible elsewhere. Researchers, including Hlouchová, have used protein design tools to show that the six amino acids found on the asteroid Bennu can create [many different types of protein folds (opens a new tab)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-71509-6).

“The origin of life is very strongly connected to planetary exploration, and we should always think of this as, you know, we’re trying to understand the nature of life in the universe,” Barge said. “We need to understand the origin of life in order to effectively look for life.”

Kaçar, director of the NASA Interdisciplinary Astrobiology Research center, is leading the way in connecting the two fields. Her lab uses synthetic biology and computational methods to predict the genetic codes of ancient proteins and resurrect them inside modern bacteria. Then she monitors their activity to see what kind of patterns they might leave behind in ancient rocks. By bridging the dynamics of a molecule, its geological output, and its atmospheric impact, she’s hoping to identify biosignatures that could be used to search for life in the cosmos.

NASA’s [Habitable Worlds Observatory (opens a new tab)](https://science.nasa.gov/astrophysics/programs/habitable-worlds-observatory/), launching in the 2040s, will be the first space telescope specifically designed to search for biosignatures in the atmospheres of planets outside our solar system. And the European Space Agency’s upcoming space telescope [Plato (opens a new tab)](https://www.esa.int/missions/about-us/directorates/science/plato) will also be looking. Barge hopes that they will find not only clear evidence of life beyond Earth but also clues to how it began. This “is not something you can ever see on Earth because it’s all been overprinted by life,” she said.

Evidence of life elsewhere could be the key to finally dissolving the arguments and rifts that have haunted this field since its beginning. Through all these decades, scientists have theorized about the emergence of a system for which we have only one example: life on Earth. No matter how imaginative they get, scientific ideas about the origins of life remain constrained by the singular model that emerged from the prebiotic soup more than 4 billion years ago.

Scientists are now closer than ever, in the lab or deep in space, to increasing the sample size in the experiment of life. One day, there could be two.

# Pablo Neruda on How to Hold Time

### By Maria Popova

[![Image 35: Pablo Neruda on How to Hold Time](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/essentialneruda.jpg?fit=320%2C505&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Essential-Neruda-Selected-Bilingual-English/dp/0872864286/?tag=braipick-20)

“Time is a river that sweeps me along, but I am a river,” Borges [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/09/19/a-new-refutation-of-time-borges/). “Time is a fire that consumes me, but I am the fire.”

Most of us are not Borges. Most of us are drowning in bewilderment at [where the time goes](https://www.themarginalian.org/2017/02/21/nina-simone-time/), burning with the urgency of being alive while [waiting to start living](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/10/17/henry-james-the-beast-in-the-jungle/), wandering the labyrinth of life with wayward presence, wishing that [time ran differently](https://www.themarginalian.org/2026/01/02/begin-again/) as the cult of productivity turns each minute into a blade pressed against the vein of our transience.

And all the while, our time is nested within our times — the epoch we are living through together, born into it with no more choice in the matter than the body and brain and family we have been born into. In his [magnificent essay on Shakespeare](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/11/11/james-baldwin-shakespeare-language-poetry/), James Baldwin countered the commonplace lament of every epoch: “It is said that his time was easier than ours, but I doubt it — no time can be easy if one is living through it.” A century before him — a century of unrest and transformation — Emerson issued the ultimate antilamentation: “This time, like all times, is a very good one, if we but know what to do with it.”

[![Image 36](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/07/DiscusChronologicus_small.jpg?resize=680%2C728&ssl=1)](https://society6.com/product/discus-chronologicus-german-time-model-from-the-1720s_print?curator=brainpicker)

_Discus chronologicus_ — a German depiction of time from the early 1720s. (Available as [a print](https://society6.com/product/discus-chronologicus-german-time-model-from-the-1720s_print?curator=brainpicker) and as [a wall clock](https://society6.com/product/discus-chronologicus-german-time-model-from-the-1720s_wall-clock?curator=brainpicker).)

Not knowing what to do with the time we have been given, not knowing how to hold time in our personal and political lives, is at bottom an act of forgetting how time hold us. [Pablo Neruda](https://www.themarginalian.org/tag/pablo-neruda/) (July 12, 1904–September 23, 1973) casts a spell against forgetting in the fourth canto of his long poem “Morning,”:

> You will remember that whimsical ravine  
>  where the vibrant aromas rose,  
>  and from time to time a bird dressed  
>  in water and languor: winter’s garment.
> 
> 
> You will remember those gifts from the earth:  
>  piquing fragrance, gold clay,  
>  thickets of herbs, wild roots,  
>  bewitching thorns like swords.
> 
> 
> You will remember the bouquet you brought,  
>  a bouquet of shadow and silent water,  
>  a bouquet like foam-covered stone.
> 
> 
> And that time was like never and always:  
>  We go where nothing is expected  
>  and find everything waiting there.

[![Image 37](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/pabloneruda_young.jpg?resize=680%2C402&ssl=1)](https://www.amazon.com/Essential-Neruda-Selected-Bilingual-English/dp/0872864286/?tag=braipick-20)

Pablo Neruda

If time is the fundamental problem of human life and poetry is our most precise technology for parsing the aching astonishment of being alive, then time is the prime subject of poetry. Neruda knew this — time is the subterranean current coursing beneath his vast and varied body of work, the substrate upon which all of his [stunning love poems](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/11/19/neruda-si-tu-me-olvidas/) and his [meditations on the inner life](https://www.themarginalian.org/2015/05/28/keeping-quiet-sylvia-boorstein-reads-pablo-neruda/) grow. He reverenced the stones for how they have “touched time,” reverenced the minute for how it is “bound to join the river of time that bears us,” reverenced “the inexhaustible springs of time,” longed for “a time complete as an ocean,” then made that ocean with his poetry.

In his poem “The Enigmas,” composed during WWII, he writes:

> You’ve asked me what the crustacean spins  
>  between its gold claws  
>  and I reply: the sea knows.
> 
> 
> You wonder what the sea squirt waits for in its transparent bell?  
> What does it wait for?
> 
> 
> I’ll tell you: it’s waiting for time like you.

A decade later, in one of his “Elemental Odes,” Neruda laid out his most explicit instruction for how to hold time:

> Listen and learn.  
>  Time  
>  is divided  
>  into two rivers:  
>  one  
>  flows backward, devouring  
>  life already lived;  
>  the other  
>  moves forward with you  
>  exposing  
>  your life.  
>  For a single second  
>  they may be joined.  
>  Now.  
>  This is that moment,  
>  the drop of an instant  
>  that washes away the past.  
>  It is the present.  
>  It is in your hands.  
>  Racing, slipping,  
>  tumbling like a waterfall.  
>  But it is yours.  
>  Help it grow  
>  with love, with firmness,  
>  with stone and flight,  
>  with resounding  
>  rectitude,  
>  with purest grains,  
>  the most brilliant metal  
>  from your heart,  
>  walking  
>  in the full light of day  
>  without fear  
>  of truth, goodness, justice,  
>  companions of song,  
>  time that flows  
>  will have the shape  
>  and sound  
>  of a guitar,  
>  and when you want  
>  to bow to the past,  
>  the singing spring of  
>  transparent time  
>  will reveal your wholeness.  
>  Time is joy.

Couple with [three poems for trusting time](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/06/21/stone-time/), then revisit Kahlil Gibran on [how to befriend time](https://www.themarginalian.org/2020/01/05/kahlil-gibran-prophet-time/).

# What Makes You Yourself: Posidonia Australis, Pando, and the Paradox of Personhood

### By Maria Popova

> [Bigger than Manhattan, Earth’s largest living organism sways in the surf south of Australia: _Posidonia australis_ — a species of seagrass that, unable to flower, clones itself. Older than mathematics and the written word, it has been cloning itself since before the pyramids were built — a kind of immortality. And while I kiss my lover on the fresh-cut grass under the Manhattan Bridge, it goes on cloning itself as we go on dying and passing between our lips the heat of our mortality.](https://www.themarginalian.org/traversal/)

An organism is a mortal unit of matter distinct from other organisms by its genome — the possibilities encoded in its particular genetic makeup — and its phenotype — the set of traits expressed, the actualities summoned by adaptation and chance from its possibilities. Human beings are organisms encased in the hardest yet most vulnerable exoskeleton in nature: a self. A self includes but surpasses the organism to encompass its environment and its social context, the psychological terrain of memory and desire, the fingerprints left on it by the touch of other selves. An organism ends at the physical boundary of its body, but a self does not — we spend our lives negotiating where we end and the world begins.

[![Image 34](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/StellersJay_becoming.jpg)](https://almanacofbirds.org/)

Card from _[An Almanac of Birds: 100 Divinations for Uncertain Days](https://almanacofbirds.org/)_.

Humans are the only animals, save perhaps [the bowerbird](https://www.themarginalian.org/2023/10/29/bowerbird), who can alter their phenotype by means of their own making — grow, cut, and dye their hair, tattoo and tan their skin, increase and decrease the size of various body parts with scalpel and silicone. We are also the only animal who can radically alter both its environment and its social context, building elaborate homes on faraway landmasses, reconstituting our families and friend groups, changing the labors by which we put food on our table. Our selves are not like our cells, replacing themselves with clones in the course of living, but like Russian nesting dolls, each prior self outgrown but contained by the next. (“We are well advised to keep on nodding terms with the people we used to be, whether we find them attractive company or not,” Joan Didion [wrote](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/11/19/joan-didion-on-keeping-a-notebook/).) Our lives a relay race, running from the selves we have outgrown or wish to outgrow towards the selves we try to become to or are unconsciously becoming, the baton of personhood passed from one to the next along the arrow of time, the track of our mortality.

This puts us in a peculiar predicament: Each human lifetime is lived by a single organism that contains a multitude of selves, genetically continuous and psychologically discontinuous, making it impossible to define where and what the person is. What, then, makes you yourself across all those replaced cells and reconfigured selves?

Organisms like _Posidonia australis_, which both conceal and reveal the nature of the self, may give us the best hint at an answer — one which evolutionary biologist Rowan Hooper articulates beautifully in his book [**_Togetherness: Symbiosis and the Hidden Story of Life’s Greatest Collaborations_**](https://www.amazon.com/dp/0593802667/?tag=braipick-20) ([_public library_](https://search.worldcat.org/title/1621330382)). Considering Earth’s largest living tree, he writes:

> The Pando aspen grove in Utah comprises 47,000 trees, all genetically identical, connected by a vast root system. Language immediately becomes limiting when trying to describe Pando. Do we call the forest an organism? An entity? It has been estimated to weigh nearly 6 million kilograms, or 6,000 tonnes. If it helps, that’s about thirty-five blue whales or 1,000 elephants. It is one of the oldest organisms on Earth. Its cells are living and dying over time, but the DNA remains pretty much unchanged. That is, the entity lives on, even as its parts die.

[![Image 35](https://i0.wp.com/www.themarginalian.org/wp-content/uploads/2022/12/meredithnemirov_riverstrees9.jpg?w=1000&ssl=1)](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/12/04/rivers-feed-the-trees-meredith-nemirov/)

Art by [Meredith Nemirov](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/12/04/rivers-feed-the-trees-meredith-nemirov/)

With an eye to [the Ship of Theseus](https://www.themarginalian.org/2016/03/08/plutarch-the-ship-of-theseus-ted-ed/) — Plutarch’s timeless thought experiment about the nature of the self — he reflects:

> Pando is biology’s Ship of Theseus — is it the same tree as when it first sprouted? I think not. It’s more like a continuation of the _idea_ of Pando… The 47,000 stems of Pando start off genetically the same, but grow phenotypically different; a forest, but also a mass of individuals.

“The word for world is forest,” Ursula K. Le Guin wrote in her subtle insistence that symbiosis — [the ultimate unselfing of the organism](https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/12/21/lynn-margulis-symbiotic-planet/) — is what made this rocky planet a living world. Rustling through the canopy of the Pando is the whisper of an answer to the unnerving question of what makes a body a person: You are not your roots, not the stem of your circumstance, not your branching choices. You are the idea of you, the forest of your selves in constant conviviality with other selves, called again and again to [unself into who you really are](https://www.themarginalian.org/2025/09/25/fernando-pessoa-disquiet-self/).
